claim: In electroreceptive jawed fishes and amphibians, individual lateral line placodes form lines of neuromasts on the head containing mechanosensory hair cells, flanked by fields of ampullary organs containing electroreceptors.
source: In electroreceptive jawed fishes and amphibians, individual lateral line placodes form lines of neuromasts on the head containing mechanosensory hair cells, flanked by fields of ampullary organs containing electroreceptors—modified hair cells that respond to weak electric fields.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the anatomical organization of the lateral line system in electroreceptive vertebrates, supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Electroreceptors are modified hair cells that respond to weak electric fields.
source: In electroreceptive jawed fishes and amphibians, individual lateral line placodes form lines of neuromasts on the head containing mechanosensory hair cells, flanked by fields of ampullary organs containing electroreceptors—modified hair cells that respond to weak electric fields.
evidence: This characterization of electroreceptors is based on established scientific knowledge about their function and evolutionary relationship to hair cells.

claim: Extensively shared gene expression between neuromasts and ampullary organs suggests that conserved molecular mechanisms are involved in their development.
source: Extensively shared gene expression between neuromasts and ampullary organs suggests that conserved molecular mechanisms are involved in their development, but a few transcription factor genes are restricted either to the developing electrosensory or mechanosensory lateral line.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from observed gene expression patterns reported in previous studies and in this manuscript.

claim: A few transcription factor genes are restricted either to the developing electrosensory or mechanosensory lateral line.
source: Extensively shared gene expression between neuromasts and ampullary organs suggests that conserved molecular mechanisms are involved in their development, but a few transcription factor genes are restricted either to the developing electrosensory or mechanosensory lateral line.
evidence: This statement is supported by gene expression data presented in this study and previous work by the authors.

claim: Atoh1 is required for both hair cell and electroreceptor differentiation in sterlet.
source: We found that the 'hair cell' transcription factor gene Atoh1 is required for both hair cell and electroreceptor differentiation in sterlet, and for Pou4f3 and Gfi1 expression in both neuromasts and ampullary organs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis experiments showing loss of hair cells and electroreceptors in Atoh1 crispants.

claim: Atoh1 is required for Pou4f3 and Gfi1 expression in both neuromasts and ampullary organs in sterlet.
source: We found that the 'hair cell' transcription factor gene Atoh1 is required for both hair cell and electroreceptor differentiation in sterlet, and for Pou4f3 and Gfi1 expression in both neuromasts and ampullary organs.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing loss of Pou4f3 and Gfi1 expression in Atoh1 crispants.

claim: The data support the conservation of developmental mechanisms between hair cells and electroreceptors.
source: These data support the conservation of developmental mechanisms between hair cells and electroreceptors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing that Atoh1 is required for both hair cell and electroreceptor development.

claim: Targeting ampullary organ-restricted Neurod4 did not yield any phenotype.
source: Targeting ampullary organ-restricted Neurod4 did not yield any phenotype, potentially owing to redundancy with other Neurod genes that we found to be expressed in sterlet ampullary organs.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis of Neurod4 showing no detectable phenotype.

claim: The lack of Neurod4 phenotype is potentially owing to redundancy with other Neurod genes that are expressed in sterlet ampullary organs.
source: Targeting ampullary organ-restricted Neurod4 did not yield any phenotype, potentially owing to redundancy with other Neurod genes that we found to be expressed in sterlet ampullary organs.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of phenotype, supported by gene expression data showing other Neurod family members in ampullary organs.

claim: After targeting mechanosensory-restricted Foxg1, ampullary organs formed within neuromast lines.
source: After targeting mechanosensory-restricted Foxg1, ampullary organs formed within neuromast lines, suggesting that FoxG1 normally represses their development, whether directly or indirectly.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis showing ectopic ampullary organs in neuromast lines of Foxg1 crispants.

claim: FoxG1 normally represses ampullary organ development, whether directly or indirectly.
source: After targeting mechanosensory-restricted Foxg1, ampullary organs formed within neuromast lines, suggesting that FoxG1 normally represses their development, whether directly or indirectly.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that ampullary organs form ectopically in neuromast lines when Foxg1 is disrupted.

claim: Electrosensory organs may be the 'default' developmental fate of lateral line primordia in electroreceptive vertebrates.
source: We speculate that electrosensory organs may be the 'default' developmental fate of lateral line primordia in electroreceptive vertebrates.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observation that ampullary organs form when Foxg1 is disrupted.

claim: Mechanosensory hair cells in different compartments of the inner ear transduce fluid movements for hearing and balance.
source: Mechanosensory hair cells in different compartments of the inner ear transduce fluid movements for hearing and balance (Moser et al., 2020; Caprara and Peng, 2022; Mukhopadhyay and Pangrsic, 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on hair cell function.

claim: In fishes and aquatic-stage amphibians, hair cells are found in lateral line neuromasts in the skin, which are stimulated by local water movement.
source: In fishes and aquatic-stage amphibians, hair cells are also found in lateral line neuromasts in the skin, which are stimulated by local water movement (Mogdans, 2019; Webb, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on lateral line function.

claim: Supporting cells in neuromasts differentiate into hair cells for homeostasis and repair.
source: Supporting cells in neuromasts differentiate into hair cells for homeostasis and repair (Kniss et al., 2016; Lush et al., 2019) and neuromasts are easily accessible in lines over the head and trunk, making the zebrafish lateral line an excellent model for hair cell development and regeneration (Kniss et al., 2016; Nicolson, 2017; Pickett and Raible, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on hair cell regeneration.

claim: The zebrafish lateral line is an excellent model for hair cell development and regeneration.
source: Supporting cells in neuromasts differentiate into hair cells for homeostasis and repair (Kniss et al., 2016; Lush et al., 2019) and neuromasts are easily accessible in lines over the head and trunk, making the zebrafish lateral line an excellent model for hair cell development and regeneration (Kniss et al., 2016; Nicolson, 2017; Pickett and Raible, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature and the accessibility of neuromasts in zebrafish.

claim: The lateral line system of zebrafish is purely mechanosensory.
source: The lateral line system of zebrafish (a cyprinid teleost) is purely mechanosensory, as is the lateral line system of the other main anamniote lab model, the frog Xenopus.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about zebrafish lateral line anatomy and function.

claim: The lateral line system of Xenopus is purely mechanosensory.
source: The lateral line system of zebrafish (a cyprinid teleost) is purely mechanosensory, as is the lateral line system of the other main anamniote lab model, the frog Xenopus.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about Xenopus lateral line anatomy and function.

claim: In many other vertebrates, the lateral line system has an electrosensory division.
source: However, in many other vertebrates, the lateral line system also has an electrosensory division (Bullock et al., 1983; Baker et al., 2013; Crampton, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on electroreception.

claim: In electroreceptive non-teleost jawed vertebrates, some or all of the neuromast lines on the head are flanked by fields of ampullary organs containing electroreceptors.
source: In electroreceptive non-teleost jawed vertebrates, some or all of the neuromast lines on the head are flanked by fields of ampullary organs containing electroreceptors, which respond to weak cathodal stimuli such as the electric fields surrounding other animals in water (Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005; Crampton, 2019; Leitch and Julius, 2019; Chagnaud et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on electroreceptor anatomy and distribution.

claim: Electroreceptors respond to weak cathodal stimuli such as the electric fields surrounding other animals in water.
source: In electroreceptive non-teleost jawed vertebrates, some or all of the neuromast lines on the head are flanked by fields of ampullary organs containing electroreceptors, which respond to weak cathodal stimuli such as the electric fields surrounding other animals in water (Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005; Crampton, 2019; Leitch and Julius, 2019; Chagnaud et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on electroreceptor function.

claim: Electroreception is mediated by voltage-gated calcium channels in the apical membrane.
source: Electroreception is mediated by voltage-gated calcium channels in the apical membrane (Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005; Leitch and Julius, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on electroreceptor physiology.

claim: The voltage sensor in cartilaginous fishes was recently identified as the L-type voltage-gated calcium channel Cav1.3.
source: The voltage sensor was recently identified in cartilaginous fishes as the L-type voltage-gated calcium channel Cav1.3 (Bellono et al., 2017; Bellono et al., 2018), whose pore-forming alpha subunit is encoded by Cacna1d.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent research identifying the voltage sensor in electroreceptors.

claim: The pore-forming alpha subunit of Cav1.3 is encoded by Cacna1d.
source: The voltage sensor was recently identified in cartilaginous fishes as the L-type voltage-gated calcium channel Cav1.3 (Bellono et al., 2017; Bellono et al., 2018), whose pore-forming alpha subunit is encoded by Cacna1d.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about the molecular composition of Cav1.3 channels.

claim: Cav1.3 is required for synaptic transmission at hair-cell ribbon synapses.
source: Cav1.3 is also required for synaptic transmission at hair-cell ribbon synapses (Moser et al., 2020; Mukhopadhyay and Pangrsic, 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on hair cell synaptic function.

claim: Electroreceptors, like hair cells, have an apical primary cilium and basolateral ribbon synapses with lateral line afferents.
source: Electroreceptors, like hair cells, have an apical primary cilium and basolateral ribbon synapses with lateral line afferents (Jørgensen, 2005; Baker, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to literature describing the ultrastructure of electroreceptors and hair cells.

claim: Hair cells have a highly ordered, stepped array of apical microvilli ('stereocilia') that forms the 'hair bundle' critical for hair-cell mechanotransduction.
source: However, in contrast to the highly ordered, stepped array of apical microvilli ('stereocilia') that forms the 'hair bundle' critical for hair-cell mechanotransduction (Caprara and Peng, 2022), electroreceptors in many species (for example, cartilaginous fishes; ray-finned paddlefishes and sturgeons) lack apical microvilli altogether (Jørgensen, 2005; Baker, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature on hair cell structure and function.

claim: Electroreceptors in many species (for example, cartilaginous fishes; ray-finned paddlefishes and sturgeons) lack apical microvilli altogether.
source: However, in contrast to the highly ordered, stepped array of apical microvilli ('stereocilia') that forms the 'hair bundle' critical for hair-cell mechanotransduction (Caprara and Peng, 2022), electroreceptors in many species (for example, cartilaginous fishes; ray-finned paddlefishes and sturgeons) lack apical microvilli altogether (Jørgensen, 2005; Baker, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to literature describing electroreceptor ultrastructure in different species.

claim: Electroreceptors in some species have a few apical microvilli.
source: Electroreceptors in other species have a few apical microvilli, while the electroreceptors of the amphibian axolotl have around 200 microvilli surrounding an eccentrically positioned primary cilium (Jørgensen, 2005; Baker, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to literature describing electroreceptor ultrastructure in different species.

claim: The electroreceptors of the amphibian axolotl have around 200 microvilli surrounding an eccentrically positioned primary cilium.
source: Electroreceptors in other species have a few apical microvilli, while the electroreceptors of the amphibian axolotl have around 200 microvilli surrounding an eccentrically positioned primary cilium (Jørgensen, 2005; Baker, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to literature describing axolotl electroreceptor ultrastructure.

claim: Axolotl electroreceptors were described as 'remarkably similar to immature hair cells'.
source: Indeed, axolotl electroreceptors were described as "remarkably similar to immature hair cells" (Northcutt et al., 1994).
evidence: This statement is a direct quote from a cited publication.

claim: The apical surface of electroreceptors varies considerably across different vertebrate groups.
source: Thus, despite their shared function, the apical surface of electroreceptors (where voltage-sensing occurs; Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005; Leitch and Julius, 2019) varies considerably across different vertebrate groups.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the described variation in electroreceptor ultrastructure across species.

claim: Voltage-sensing in electroreceptors occurs at the apical surface.
source: Thus, despite their shared function, the apical surface of electroreceptors (where voltage-sensing occurs; Bodznick and Montgomery, 2005; Leitch and Julius, 2019) varies considerably across different vertebrate groups.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to literature on electroreceptor physiology.

claim: Fate-mapping experiments have shown that neuromasts, ampullary organs (where present) and their afferent neurons all develop from a series of pre-otic and post-otic lateral line placodes on the embryonic head.
source: Fate-mapping experiments have shown that neuromasts, ampullary organs (where present) and their afferent neurons all develop from a series of pre-otic and post-otic lateral line placodes on the embryonic head (Northcutt, 1997; Piotrowski and Baker, 2014; Baker, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to fate-mapping studies.

claim: In electroreceptive jawed vertebrates, lateral line placodes elongate to form sensory ridges that eventually fragment.
source: In electroreceptive jawed vertebrates, lateral line placodes elongate to form sensory ridges that eventually fragment: neuromasts differentiate first, in a line along the centre of each ridge, and ampullary organs (if present) form later, in fields on the flanks of the ridge (Northcutt, 1997; Piotrowski and Baker, 2014; Baker, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to developmental studies of the lateral line system.

claim: Neuromasts differentiate first, in a line along the centre of each sensory ridge.
source: In electroreceptive jawed vertebrates, lateral line placodes elongate to form sensory ridges that eventually fragment: neuromasts differentiate first, in a line along the centre of each ridge, and ampullary organs (if present) form later, in fields on the flanks of the ridge (Northcutt, 1997; Piotrowski and Baker, 2014; Baker, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to developmental studies of the lateral line system.

claim: Ampullary organs form later, in fields on the flanks of the sensory ridge.
source: In electroreceptive jawed vertebrates, lateral line placodes elongate to form sensory ridges that eventually fragment: neuromasts differentiate first, in a line along the centre of each ridge, and ampullary organs (if present) form later, in fields on the flanks of the ridge (Northcutt, 1997; Piotrowski and Baker, 2014; Baker, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to developmental studies of the lateral line system.

claim: A variety of genes are expressed in developing ampullary organs as well as neuromasts in embryos from cartilaginous fishes, lobe-finned bony fishes/tetrapods, and ray-finned bony fishes.
source: This enabled us to identify a variety of genes expressed in developing ampullary organs as well as neuromasts, in embryos from the three major jawed-vertebrate groups, that is, cartilaginous fishes (lesser-spotted catshark, Scyliorhinus canicula, and little skate, Leucoraja erinacea; O'Neill et al., 2007; Gillis et al., 2012); lobe-finned bony fishes/tetrapods (a urodele amphibian, the axolotl, Ambystoma mexicanum; Modrell and Baker, 2012); and ray-finned bony fishes (a chondrostean, the Mississippi paddlefish, Polyodon spathula; Modrell et al., 2011a; Modrell et al., 2011b; Modrell et al., 2017b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous gene expression studies by the authors.

claim: Differential bulk RNA-seq in late-larval paddlefish yielded a dataset of almost 500 genes that were putatively enriched in lateral line organs.
source: We also took an unbiased discovery approach using differential bulk RNA-seq in late-larval paddlefish, which yielded a dataset of almost 500 genes that were putatively enriched in lateral line organs (Modrell et al., 2017a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous RNA-seq study by the authors.

claim: Validation by in situ hybridisation of a subset of candidates from the RNA-seq dataset suggested that conserved molecular mechanisms were involved in hair cell and electroreceptor development.
source: Validation by in situ hybridisation (ISH) of a subset of candidates from this dataset suggested that conserved molecular mechanisms were involved in hair cell and electroreceptor development, and that hair cells and electroreceptors were closely related physiologically (Modrell et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from gene expression validation studies cited in the text.

claim: Hair cells and electroreceptors are closely related physiologically.
source: Validation by in situ hybridisation (ISH) of a subset of candidates from this dataset suggested that conserved molecular mechanisms were involved in hair cell and electroreceptor development, and that hair cells and electroreceptors were closely related physiologically (Modrell et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from gene expression validation studies cited in the text.

claim: Developing ampullary organs express the key 'hair cell' transcription factor genes Atoh1 and Pou4f3.
source: For example, developing ampullary organs express the key 'hair cell' transcription factor genes Atoh1 and Pou4f3 (see Roccio et al., 2020; Iyer and Groves, 2021), and genes essential for the function of hair cell ribbon synapses, including the voltage-gated calcium channel gene Cacna1d, encoding Cav1.3 (Modrell et al., 2017a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to gene expression studies.

claim: Developing ampullary organs express genes essential for the function of hair cell ribbon synapses, including Cacna1d.
source: For example, developing ampullary organs express the key 'hair cell' transcription factor genes Atoh1 and Pou4f3 (see Roccio et al., 2020; Iyer and Groves, 2021), and genes essential for the function of hair cell ribbon synapses, including the voltage-gated calcium channel gene Cacna1d, encoding Cav1.3 (Modrell et al., 2017a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to gene expression studies.

claim: Two electroreceptor-specific voltage-gated potassium channel subunit genes (Kcna5 and Kcnab3) are expressed in developing ampullary organs but not neuromasts.
source: We also identified a handful of genes expressed in developing ampullary organs but not neuromasts, including two electroreceptor-specific voltage-gated potassium channel subunit genes (Kcna5 and Kcnab3) and a single transcription factor gene, Neurod4 (Modrell et al., 2017a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous gene expression study by the authors.

claim: Neurod4 is a transcription factor gene expressed in developing ampullary organs but not neuromasts.
source: We also identified a handful of genes expressed in developing ampullary organs but not neuromasts, including two electroreceptor-specific voltage-gated potassium channel subunit genes (Kcna5 and Kcnab3) and a single transcription factor gene, Neurod4 (Modrell et al., 2017a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous gene expression study by the authors.

claim: Fifteen transcription factor genes have shared expression in both ampullary organs and neuromasts.
source: Up to that point, we had reported the shared expression of fifteen transcription factor genes in both ampullary organs and neuromasts, but only one transcription factor gene with restricted expression, namely, electrosensory-restricted Neurod4 (Modrell et al., 2011a; Modrell et al., 2011b; Modrell et al., 2017a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous gene expression studies by the authors.

claim: 23 more transcription factor genes were identified as expressed within developing lateral line organs in paddlefish and/or sterlet.
source: More recently (Minařík et al., 2024), we used the late-larval paddlefish lateral line organ-enriched dataset (Modrell et al., 2017a), as well as a candidate gene approach, to identify 23 more transcription factor genes expressed within developing lateral line organs in paddlefish and/or in a related, more experimentally tractable chondrostean, the sterlet (Acipenser ruthenus, a small sturgeon; for example, Chen et al., 2018; Baloch et al., 2019; Stundl et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent publication by the authors.

claim: Twelve transcription factor genes including Gfi1 are expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts.
source: Twelve of these transcription factor genes—including Gfi1—were expressed in both ampullary organs and neuromasts (Minařík et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent publication by the authors.

claim: Developing ampullary organs and neuromasts express the three 'hair cell' transcription factor genes Atoh1, Pou4f3, and Gfi1.
source: Thus, developing ampullary organs, as well as neuromasts, express the three 'hair cell' transcription factor genes—Atoh1, Pou4f3, and Gfi1—whose co-expression is sufficient to drive postnatal mouse cochlear supporting cells to adopt a 'hair cell-like' fate, albeit not to form fully mature hair cells (Roccio et al., 2020; Iyer and Groves, 2021; Chen et al., 2021; Iyer et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to gene expression studies and functional studies in mouse.

claim: Co-expression of Atoh1, Pou4f3, and Gfi1 is sufficient to drive postnatal mouse cochlear supporting cells to adopt a 'hair cell-like' fate, albeit not to form fully mature hair cells.
source: Thus, developing ampullary organs, as well as neuromasts, express the three 'hair cell' transcription factor genes—Atoh1, Pou4f3, and Gfi1—whose co-expression is sufficient to drive postnatal mouse cochlear supporting cells to adopt a 'hair cell-like' fate, albeit not to form fully mature hair cells (Roccio et al., 2020; Iyer and Groves, 2021; Chen et al., 2021; Iyer et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to functional studies in mouse.

claim: Six novel ampullary organ-restricted transcription factor genes were identified.
source: We also identified six novel ampullary organ-restricted transcription factor genes and the first-reported mechanosensory-restricted transcription factor genes (Minařík et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent publication by the authors.

claim: The first-reported mechanosensory-restricted transcription factor genes were identified.
source: We also identified six novel ampullary organ-restricted transcription factor genes and the first-reported mechanosensory-restricted transcription factor genes (Minařík et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent publication by the authors.

claim: Foxg1 is one of five mechanosensory-restricted transcription factor genes.
source: One of the five mechanosensory-restricted transcription factor genes was Foxg1, which was expressed and maintained in the central region of sensory ridges where lines of neuromasts form, although excluded from hair cells (Minařík et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent publication by the authors.

claim: Foxg1 is expressed and maintained in the central region of sensory ridges where lines of neuromasts form, although excluded from hair cells.
source: One of the five mechanosensory-restricted transcription factor genes was Foxg1, which was expressed and maintained in the central region of sensory ridges where lines of neuromasts form, although excluded from hair cells (Minařík et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent publication by the authors showing gene expression patterns.

claim: Targeting Foxg1 resulted in the ectopic formation of ampullary organs within neuromast lines.
source: Targeting mechanosensory-restricted Foxg1 resulted in a striking phenotype: the ectopic formation of ampullary organs within neuromast lines, and in some cases the fusion of ampullary organ fields that normally develop either side of a line of neuromasts.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data from CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis showing ectopic ampullary organs in Foxg1 crispants.

claim: Targeting Foxg1 resulted in the fusion of ampullary organ fields that normally develop either side of a line of neuromasts in some cases.
source: Targeting mechanosensory-restricted Foxg1 resulted in a striking phenotype: the ectopic formation of ampullary organs within neuromast lines, and in some cases the fusion of ampullary organ fields that normally develop either side of a line of neuromasts.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data from CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis showing fusion of ampullary organ fields in Foxg1 crispants.

claim: Sections of neuromast lines were often missing mosaically in Foxg1 crispants.
source: In addition, sections of neuromast lines were often missing mosaically, supporting a direct role for FoxG1 in neuromast development, as recently reported in zebrafish (Bell et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data from CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis showing missing neuromasts in Foxg1 crispants.

claim: The missing neuromasts in Foxg1 crispants support a direct role for FoxG1 in neuromast development.
source: In addition, sections of neuromast lines were often missing mosaically, supporting a direct role for FoxG1 in neuromast development, as recently reported in zebrafish (Bell et al., 2024).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observation of missing neuromasts in Foxg1 crispants, supported by a citation to a recent zebrafish study.

claim: FoxG1 has a direct role in neuromast development in zebrafish.
source: In addition, sections of neuromast lines were often missing mosaically, supporting a direct role for FoxG1 in neuromast development, as recently reported in zebrafish (Bell et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent zebrafish study.

claim: The presence of ectopic ampullary organs within neuromast lines in Foxg1 crispants suggests that ampullary organs may be the 'default' developmental fate for lateral line sensory ridges.
source: However, the presence of ectopic ampullary organs within neuromast lines in Foxg1 crispants suggests the unexpected but intriguing hypothesis that ampullary organs may be the 'default' developmental fate for lateral line sensory ridges, and that this is repressed by FoxG1, allowing neuromasts to form instead.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the experimental observation of ectopic ampullary organs in Foxg1 crispants.

claim: FoxG1 represses the default ampullary organ fate, allowing neuromasts to form instead.
source: However, the presence of ectopic ampullary organs within neuromast lines in Foxg1 crispants suggests the unexpected but intriguing hypothesis that ampullary organs may be the 'default' developmental fate for lateral line sensory ridges, and that this is repressed by FoxG1, allowing neuromasts to form instead.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the experimental observation of ectopic ampullary organs in Foxg1 crispants.

claim: Sox2 is a supporting cell marker in sterlet lateral line organs.
source: Immunostaining for the supporting cell marker Sox2 at stage 45 shows strong expression in neuromasts and much weaker expression in ampullary organs.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Sox2 shows strong expression in neuromasts and much weaker expression in ampullary organs at stage 45 in sterlet.
source: Immunostaining for the supporting cell marker Sox2 at stage 45 shows strong expression in neuromasts and much weaker expression in ampullary organs.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Cacna1d is a hair cell and electroreceptor marker in sterlet.
source: In situ hybridisation (ISH) for the hair cell and electroreceptor marker Cacna1d at stage 45 shows expression in neuromasts and ampullary organs.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Cacna1d shows expression in neuromasts and ampullary organs at stage 45 in sterlet.
source: In situ hybridisation (ISH) for the hair cell and electroreceptor marker Cacna1d at stage 45 shows expression in neuromasts and ampullary organs.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Kcnab3 is an electroreceptor marker in sterlet.
source: ISH for the electroreceptor marker Kcnab3 at stage 45 shows expression in ampullary organs only.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Kcnab3 shows expression in ampullary organs only at stage 45 in sterlet.
source: ISH for the electroreceptor marker Kcnab3 at stage 45 shows expression in ampullary organs only.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Atoh1 shows expression in ampullary organs and, more weakly, in neuromasts at stage 42 in sterlet.
source: ISH for Atoh1 at stage 42 shows expression in ampullary organs and, more weakly, in neuromasts.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1G,H.

claim: Neurod4 shows expression in ampullary organs but not neuromasts at stage 45 in sterlet.
source: ISH for Neurod4 at stage 45 shows expression in ampullary organs but not neuromasts.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1I,J.

claim: Foxg1 expression is restricted to neuromast lines at stage 45 in sterlet, though excluded from the centres of neuromasts where hair cells form.
source: ISH for Foxg1 at stage 45 shows expression is restricted to neuromast lines, though excluded from the centres of neuromasts where hair cells form (compare with Sox2 expression in supporting cells in panel B, and with Cacna1d expression in hair cells in panel D).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1K,L.

claim: Ovulated sterlet eggs are very large (roughly 2.5 mm in diameter).
source: Ovulated sterlet eggs are very large (roughly 2.5 mm in diameter; Lenhardt et al., 2005) and undergo a holoblastic cleavage (Dettlaff et al., 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to literature on sterlet embryology.

claim: Sterlet eggs undergo holoblastic cleavage.
source: Ovulated sterlet eggs are very large (roughly 2.5 mm in diameter; Lenhardt et al., 2005) and undergo a holoblastic cleavage (Dettlaff et al., 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to literature on sterlet embryology.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis in G0-injected sterlet embryos has been reported.
source: (Since this project started, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis in G0-injected sterlet embryos has been reported, including by two of us, RF and MP; Chen et al., 2018; Baloch et al., 2019; Stundl et al., 2022.)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Analysis of microsatellite data originally suggested that although a whole-genome duplication had occurred in the sterlet lineage, the sterlet was likely to be a functional diploid.
source: Analysis of microsatellite data had originally suggested that although a whole-genome duplication had occurred in the sterlet lineage, the sterlet was likely to be a functional diploid (Ludwig et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a microsatellite analysis study.

claim: Analysis of the sterlet genome showed that approximately 70% of ohnologs had been retained.
source: Analysis of this genome, together with transcriptomic data, showed that approximately 70% of ohnologs (i.e., gene paralogs originating from the whole-genome duplication) had been retained and suggested a high level of functional tetraploidy (Du et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a genome analysis study.

claim: The sterlet genome analysis suggested a high level of functional tetraploidy.
source: Analysis of this genome, together with transcriptomic data, showed that approximately 70% of ohnologs (i.e., gene paralogs originating from the whole-genome duplication) had been retained and suggested a high level of functional tetraploidy (Du et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a genome analysis study.

claim: Both Tyr ohnologs have been retained in sterlet, on chromosomes 8 and 9, with 99.11% nucleotide identity in the coding sequence.

claim: The two Tyr ohnologs in sterlet have 98.81% amino acid identity.
source: Searching the reference genome for Tyr showed that both Tyr ohnologs have been retained, on chromosomes 8 and 9, with 99.11% nucleotide identity in the coding sequence (98.81% amino acid identity).
evidence: This statement is based on analysis of the sterlet reference genome.

claim: The Tyr sgRNAs target both Tyr ohnologs equally.
source: Our sgRNAs target both Tyr ohnologs equally.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequence identity between the two ohnologs and the sgRNA target sequences.

claim: At least some degree of pigment loss was seen in 63/111 Tyr crispants (56.8%) across nine independent batches.

claim: The most efficient results for CRISPR/Cas9-mediated mutagenesis in sterlet were obtained by injecting 1-cell embryos with a preassembled mix of Cas9 protein plus two chemically modified sgRNAs.
source: The most efficient results were obtained by injecting 1-cell embryos with a preassembled mix of Cas9 protein plus two chemically modified sgRNAs (purchased from Synthego) against the target gene, and subsequently maintaining the embryos at room temperature for around 6 hours.
evidence: This is based on empirical optimization of the CRISPR protocol.

claim: The time from fertilisation to completion of the first cleavage in sterlet is around 2–3 hours at room temperature.
source: The time from fertilisation to completion of the first cleavage is around 2–3 hours at room temperature, giving plenty of time for the Cas9/sgRNA complex to act before returning the embryos to colder temperatures for subsequent development.
evidence: This is based on observation of sterlet embryo development.

claim: The optimum temperature for maintaining sterlet embryos for normal development is 16°C.
source: (Sterlet are cold-water fish and the optimum temperature for maintaining embryos for normal development is 16°C.)
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about sterlet husbandry.

claim: Both Atoh1 ohnologs have been retained in sterlet, on chromosomes 1 and 2, with 91.41% nucleotide identity in the coding sequence.

evidence: This statement is based on analysis of the sterlet reference genome.

claim: The two Atoh1 ohnologs in sterlet have 84.02% amino acid identity.
source: Searching the reference genome for Atoh1 showed that both Atoh1 ohnologs have been retained, on chromosomes 1 and 2, with 91.41% nucleotide identity (and 84.02% amino acid identity) in the coding sequence.
evidence: This statement is based on analysis of the sterlet reference genome.

claim: The Atoh1 copy on chromosome 2 encodes a shorter version of the protein with a four amino acid deletion near the N-terminus (E14_G17del).
source: The copy on chromosome 2 encodes a shorter version of the protein with a four amino acid deletion near the N-terminus (E14_G17del).

claim: Atoh1 sgRNA 1 has a one-base mismatch to the shorter Atoh1 gene on chromosome 2, in position 3 of the target sequence (PAM-distal), which is unlikely to prevent successful targeting.
source: Our Atoh1 sgRNA 1 (Table 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) has a one-base mismatch to the shorter Atoh1 gene on chromosome 2, in position 3 of the target sequence (PAM-distal), which is unlikely to prevent successful targeting (Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the sgRNA sequence, genome analysis, and cited literature on sgRNA targeting specificity.

claim: Atoh1 sgRNA 2 has a two-base mismatch to the longer Atoh1 gene on chromosome 1, in positions 1 and 2 of the target sequence (PAM-distal), which is unlikely to prevent successful targeting.

evidence: This is an inference based on the sgRNA sequence, genome analysis, and knowledge of sgRNA targeting specificity.

claim: The Atoh1 sgRNAs are expected to target both Atoh1 ohnologs.
source: Thus, we expect our sgRNAs to target both Atoh1 ohnologs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sgRNA sequences and genome analysis.

claim: Cacna1d expression was absent mosaically in neuromast lines and ampullary organ fields in Atoh1 crispants (n=13/22, i.e., 59%, across five independent batches).
source: However, Cacna1d expression was absent mosaically in neuromast lines and ampullary organ fields in Atoh1 crispants (Figure 3E–J; n=13/22, i.e., 59%, across five independent batches; Supplementary file 1).

claim: Disruption of the Atoh1 gene in sterlet resulted in the failure of electroreceptor differentiation.
source: This suggested that disruption of the Atoh1 gene in sterlet resulted in the failure of hair cell differentiation (as expected from zebrafish; Millimaki et al., 2007) and also electroreceptors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the loss of Cacna1d expression in ampullary organs of Atoh1 crispants.

claim: Atoh1 is required for hair cell differentiation in zebrafish.
source: This suggested that disruption of the Atoh1 gene in sterlet resulted in the failure of hair cell differentiation (as expected from zebrafish; Millimaki et al., 2007) and also electroreceptors.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a zebrafish study.

claim: Post-ISH immunostaining for Sox2 confirmed that neuromasts had formed in Atoh1 crispants.
source: Post-ISH immunostaining for the supporting-cell marker Sox2 (Hernández et al., 2007; Modrell et al., 2017a; also see Minařík et al., 2024) confirmed that neuromasts had formed (Figure 3E1,F1; also see Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–F), so the phenotype was specific to receptor cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data showing Sox2-positive neuromasts in Atoh1 crispants.

claim: The Atoh1 crispant phenotype was specific to receptor cells.
source: Post-ISH immunostaining for the supporting-cell marker Sox2 (Hernández et al., 2007; Modrell et al., 2017a; also see Minařík et al., 2024) confirmed that neuromasts had formed (Figure 3E1,F1; also see Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–F), so the phenotype was specific to receptor cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the presence of Sox2-positive supporting cells but absence of receptor cell markers in Atoh1 crispants.

claim: Kcnab3 expression was absent mosaically in ampullary organ fields in Atoh1 crispants (n=8/13, i.e., 62%, across two independent batches).

evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from in situ hybridization in Atoh1 crispants.

claim: Pou4f3 expression was absent mosaically in ampullary organ fields and neuromast lines of Atoh1 crispants (n=13/15 larvae, i.e., 87%, across three batches).

evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from in situ hybridization in Atoh1 crispants.

claim: Gfi1 expression was absent mosaically in ampullary organ fields and neuromast lines of Atoh1 crispants (n=9/14 larvae, i.e., 64%, across four batches).
source: Similarly, ISH for Gfi1 showed no phenotype in Tyr controls (Figure 4E and F; n=0/17 across five batches; Supplementary file 1), but mosaic absence of Gfi1 in ampullary organ fields and neuromast lines of Atoh1 crispants (Figure 4G–H1; n=9/14 larvae, i.e., 64%, across four batches; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from in situ hybridization in Atoh1 crispants.

claim: Pou4f3 and Gfi1 are downstream of Atoh1 in ampullary organs as well as neuromasts.
source: Thus, these data suggest that Pou4f3 and Gfi1 are downstream of Atoh1 in ampullary organs as well as neuromasts.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the loss of Pou4f3 and Gfi1 expression in Atoh1 crispants.

claim: Around two-thirds of all Atoh1 crispants analysed showed a mosaic absence of hair cells/electroreceptors (n=43/64, i.e., 67%).
source: Overall, across all riboprobes (Cacna1d, Pou4f3, and Gfi1 labelling hair cells and electroreceptors; Kcnab3 labelling electroreceptors only), around two-thirds of all Atoh1 crispants analysed showed a mosaic absence of hair cells/electroreceptors (n=43/64, i.e., 67%; Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results across all Atoh1 crispants.

claim: Approximately three-quarters of phenotypic Atoh1 crispants had bilateral mosaic phenotypes (n=33/43, i.e., 77%).
source: Approximately three-quarters of phenotypic Atoh1 crispants had bilateral mosaic phenotypes (n=33/43, i.e., 77%; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from phenotypic scoring of Atoh1 crispants.

claim: 23% of phenotypic Atoh1 crispants had unilateral phenotypes (n=10/43).
source: The remaining crispants (n=10/43, i.e., 23%) had unilateral phenotypes.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from phenotypic scoring of Atoh1 crispants.

claim: 40% of phenotypic Atoh1 crispants were differentially affected on left and right sides of the head (n=17/43).
source: Furthermore, seven crispants with bilateral phenotypes were affected to different degrees on left and right sides of the head, hence 40% overall were differentially affected on left and right sides (n=17/43; Supplementary file 2), presumably as a result of holoblastic cleavage and CRISPR mosaicism.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from phenotypic scoring of Atoh1 crispants.

claim: 88% of individual sides of phenotypic Atoh1 crispants had a phenotype (n=76/86).
source: Ten of the 43 phenotypic crispants only had unilateral phenotypes, hence 76 out of 86 (88%) individual sides had a phenotype.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from phenotypic scoring of Atoh1 crispants.

claim: 78% of phenotypic sides in Atoh1 crispants were classed as 'severe' (n=59/76).
source: Of these, fully 78% (n=59/76) were classed as 'severe', defined as more than two-thirds of cranial hair cells/electroreceptors absent in lateral view (examples shown in Figure 3E,F,O,P, Figure 3—figure supplement 2J).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from phenotypic scoring of Atoh1 crispants.

claim: 11% of phenotypic sides in Atoh1 crispants were classed as 'moderate' (n=8/76).

evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from phenotypic scoring of Atoh1 crispants.

claim: 12% of phenotypic sides in Atoh1 crispants were classed as 'mild' (n=9/76).
source: 11% (n=8/76) were classed as 'moderate' (between one-third and two-thirds of cranial hair cells/electroreceptors absent in lateral view; example shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2I) and 12% (n=9/76) as 'mild' (less than one-third of cranial hair cells/electroreceptors absent in lateral view; example shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from phenotypic scoring of Atoh1 crispants.

claim: Atoh1 is required for the differentiation of electroreceptors as well as hair cells.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that Atoh1 is required for the differentiation of electroreceptors as well as hair cells and lies upstream of Pou4f3 and Gfi1 in ampullary organs as well as neuromasts.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing loss of electroreceptors and hair cells in Atoh1 crispants.

claim: Atoh1 lies upstream of Pou4f3 and Gfi1 in ampullary organs as well as neuromasts.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that Atoh1 is required for the differentiation of electroreceptors as well as hair cells and lies upstream of Pou4f3 and Gfi1 in ampullary organs as well as neuromasts.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing loss of Pou4f3 and Gfi1 expression in Atoh1 crispants.

claim: Neurod4 was previously identified in paddlefish as the first-reported ampullary organ-restricted transcription factor in the developing lateral line system.

claim: Sterlet Neurod4 is expressed by ampullary organs but not neuromasts.

evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1I,J.

claim: Targeting Neurod4 in sterlet embryos using nine different sgRNAs had no detectable effect on the expression of electroreceptor-specific Kcnab3 (n=0/44 across nine batches).
source: We targeted Neurod4 in sterlet embryos using nine different sgRNAs (Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), injected in eight different combinations of 1–4 different sgRNAs across 10 independent batches of 1–2-cell-stage embryos (Supplementary file 1). This had no detectable effect on the expression of electroreceptor-specific Kcnab3 (n=0/44 across nine batches, Supplementary file 1) or the hair cell/electroreceptor marker Cacna1d (n=0/4 across two batches, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from in situ hybridization in Neurod4 crispants.

claim: Targeting Neurod4 in sterlet embryos had no detectable effect on the expression of the hair cell/electroreceptor marker Cacna1d (n=0/4 across two batches).
source: We targeted Neurod4 in sterlet embryos using nine different sgRNAs (Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), injected in eight different combinations of 1–4 different sgRNAs across 10 independent batches of 1–2-cell-stage embryos (Supplementary file 1). evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from in situ hybridization in Neurod4 crispants.

claim: Both Neurod4 ohnologs have been retained in sterlet: one on chromosome 45 and the other annotated on an unplaced genomic scaffold, with 99.45% nucleotide identity in the coding sequence.

claim: The two Neurod4 ohnologs in sterlet have 99.46% amino acid identity.

evidence: This statement is based on analysis of the sterlet reference genome.

claim: The Neurod4 sgRNAs target both Neurod4 ohnologs without mismatches.
source: Our sgRNAs target both Neurod4 ohnologs without mismatches.

claim: The lack of phenotype in Neurod4 crispants suggested either that Neurod4 is not required for electroreceptor differentiation, or that it acts redundantly with other transcription factors.
source: The lack of phenotype in Neurod4 crispants (n=0/48 across all markers; Supplementary file 1), despite successful disruption of the Neurod4 gene, suggested either that Neurod4 is not required for electroreceptor differentiation, despite its restriction to ampullary organs in both paddlefish and sterlet (Modrell et al., 2017a; this paper), or that it acts redundantly with other transcription factors.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the lack of phenotype in Neurod4 crispants.

claim: In paddlefish, Neurod1 expression was restricted to developing lateral line ganglia.
source: In paddlefish, Neurod1 expression was restricted to developing lateral line ganglia (Modrell et al., 2011b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous gene expression study by the authors.

claim: Sterlet Neurod1 and Neurod6 are expressed in ampullary organs, as well as neuromasts.
source: Neurod1 and Neurod6 proved to be expressed in sterlet ampullary organs, as well as neuromasts, while Neurod2 was not expressed in either (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Sterlet Neurod2 is not expressed in ampullary organs or neuromasts.
source: Neurod1 and Neurod6 proved to be expressed in sterlet ampullary organs, as well as neuromasts, while Neurod2 was not expressed in either (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The lack of effect of CRISPR/Cas9-mediated targeting of sterlet Neurod4 is likely due to redundancy with other Neurod family transcription factors co-expressed in ampullary organs.

claim: There is at least some variation in Neurod family gene expression within the developing lateral line systems of paddlefish and sterlet.
source: Our results also show there is at least some variation in Neurod family gene expression within the developing lateral line systems of paddlefish and sterlet.

source: We recently identified Foxg1 as a mechanosensory lateral line-restricted transcription factor gene in paddlefish and sterlet (Minařík et al., 2024).

claim: The two Foxg1 ohnologs in sterlet have 99.51% amino acid identity.

claim: Neuromast lines were often interrupted by ectopic ampullary organs in Foxg1 crispants (n=8/18, i.e., 44%, across two independent batches).
source: When compared with Tyr control crispants (Figure 5A–D), a striking phenotype was seen mosaically after targeting mechanosensory-restricted Foxg1 with sgRNAs 1 and 2 (Table 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1): neuromast lines were often interrupted by ectopic ampullary organs. These were defined as Cacna1d-expressing cells present within neuromast lines in larger clusters than expected for neuromasts, resembling ampullary organs (Figure 5E–L; n=8/18, i.e., 44%, across two independent batches; Supplementary file 1), or by expression of electroreceptor-specific Kcnab3 within neuromast lines, not seen in Tyr control crispants (Figure 6A–P; n=15/24, i.e., 63%, across both batches; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from in situ hybridization in Foxg1 crispants.

claim: Expression of electroreceptor-specific Kcnab3 within neuromast lines was seen in Foxg1 crispants (n=15/24, i.e., 63%, across both batches).
source: When compared with Tyr control crispants (Figure 5A–D), a striking phenotype was seen mosaically after targeting mechanosensory-restricted Foxg1 with sgRNAs 1 and 2 (Table 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1): neuromast lines were often interrupted by ectopic ampullary organs. These were defined as Cacna1d-expressing cells present within neuromast lines in larger clusters than expected for neuromasts, resembling ampullary organs (Figure 5E–L; n=8/18, i.e., 44%, across two independent batches; Supplementary file 1), or by expression of electroreceptor-specific Kcnab3 within neuromast lines, not seen in Tyr control crispants (Figure 6A–P; n=15/24, i.e., 63%, across both batches; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from in situ hybridization in Foxg1 crispants.

claim: Targeting Foxg1 with a different pair of sgRNAs generated similar phenotypes in 7/21 crispants (33%).
source: Targeting Foxg1 with a different pair of sgRNAs (Table 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) in a different batch of embryos generated similar phenotypes, that is, the interruption of neuromast lines by ectopic ampullary organs, in 7/21 crispants (33%) overall (Cacna1d: n=0/6; Kcnab3: n=7/15; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from in situ hybridization in Foxg1 crispants.

claim: ISH for Mafa showed the mosaic presence of ampullary organs in neuromast lines and/or merging of ampullary organ fields in Foxg1 crispants (n=9/18 crispants, i.e., 50%, across two independent batches).
source: Relative to the normal ampullary organ expression of Mafa in uninjected siblings/half-siblings (sufficient Tyr control crispants were not available to test; Figure 7A-D; n=0/6 larvae within one batch; Supplementary file 1), ISH for Mafa showed the mosaic presence of ampullary organs in neuromast lines and/or merging of ampullary organ fields in Foxg1 crispants (Figure 7E–J; n=9/18 crispants, i.e., 50%, across two independent batches; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from in situ hybridization in Foxg1 crispants.

claim: ISH for Neurod4 revealed the same ectopic ampullary organ phenotype in Foxg1 crispants as seen for Cacna1d, Kcnab3, and Mafa (n=3/6 crispants, i.e., 50%, within one batch).

evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from in situ hybridization in Foxg1 crispants.

claim: In several cases, ectopic electroreceptors had formed within otherwise Kcnab3 or Mafa-negative neuromasts in Foxg1 crispants (n=7).
source: Strikingly, in several cases where small patches of Kcnab3 or Mafa-positive electroreceptors seemingly developed within uninterrupted neuromast lines, skin-mount analysis after Sox2 immunostaining showed that ectopic electroreceptors had formed within otherwise Kcnab3 or Mafa-negative neuromasts, that is, with the expected elongated morphology and stronger post-ISH Sox2 immunoreactivity of neuromasts (Figure 8A–J; n=7).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from skin-mount analysis in Foxg1 crispants.

claim: Foxg1 represses electroreceptor formation within developing neuromasts.
source: This suggests that Foxg1 also represses electroreceptor formation within developing neuromasts.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of ectopic electroreceptors within neuromasts in Foxg1 crispants.

claim: Gaps in cranial neuromast lines were seen in around half of all Foxg1 crispants (n=48/87, i.e., 55%).

evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from Sox2 immunostaining in Foxg1 crispants.

claim: The 'missing neuromasts' phenotype was most commonly seen within the otic neuromast line in Foxg1 crispants.

claim: 64% of Foxg1 crispants showed a phenotype (n=56/87).

source: In the phenotypic Foxg1 crispants, neuromast lines were interrupted by ectopic ampullary organs in 75% (n=42/56), by gaps in 86% (n=48/56) and by both in 61% (n=34/56) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from phenotypic scoring of Foxg1 crispants.

source: Electroreceptors were identified within neuromasts in 13% of phenotypic Foxg1 crispants (n=7/56; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from phenotypic scoring of Foxg1 crispants.

evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from phenotypic scoring of Foxg1 crispants.

evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from phenotypic scoring of Foxg1 crispants.

claim: The otic neuromast line was the most commonly disrupted in Foxg1 crispants (76%; n=56/74 phenotypic sides).

evidence: This is a quantitative summary of experimental results from phenotypic scoring of Foxg1 crispants.

claim: A severe phenotype was scored in 29% of disrupted otic lines in Foxg1 crispants (n=16/56).
source: The most commonly disrupted neuromast line was the otic line (76%; n=56/74 phenotypic sides of Foxg1 crispants; Figure 9B), with a severe phenotype scored in 29% of cases (n=16/56; Figure 9C).

claim: The molecular mechanisms underlying electroreceptor formation are highly conserved with those underlying hair cell formation.
source: Together with the striking conservation of transcription factor gene expression between developing ampullary organs and neuromasts (Modrell et al., 2011a; Modrell et al., 2011b; Modrell et al., 2017a; Modrell et al., 2017b; also Minařík et al., 2024), the phenotypes seen in Atoh1-targeted G0 sterlet crispants suggest that the molecular mechanisms underlying electroreceptor formation are highly conserved with those underlying hair cell formation.
